item.title: Sometimes Violence Is Actually the Answer?
item.description:
Anger

Sometimes Violence Is Actually the Answer?

For effective self-protection offense is the best defence.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Physical violence is sometimes unavoidable.
  • Self-protection requires tactical movement towards a threat in order to defeat it.
  • Always try to avoid confrontation whenever possible.
  • When it is impossible to avoid, taking the initiative is the only way out.

"Karate is for defense only," Mr. Miyagi famously told Daniel-san in "The Karate Kid." In contrast (sort of), Cobra Kai advised to "strike first, strike hard, and show no mercy." Mr Miyagi's quote seems to echo an ethos from Okinawan and Japanese traditions that advise "karate ni sente nashi"; there is no first attack. But which is correct?

Making sense of defense

The basic core of many martial arts is self-protection throughout all situations. It is key to always be aware of the unfolding situation, get out of the way of the threat by moving forward and off the direct line from the opponent to place yourself in a safe position to respond. Initially, stopping the threat may require hitting lethal targets (e.g., a punch to the throat) because your skill is not high enough. The next training stage is hitting targets to incapacitate (e.g., kicking the knee to tear ligaments) and provide an opening to escape and get away. The highest level, when actual physical exchange is inevitable, is dodging and avoiding all attacks and escaping.

I prefer the concept of self-protection rather than self-defense. Self-protection involves proactive attack, while self-defense implies waiting to be attacked and then responding. Defense encourages backing up and attacking moving forward. But if we are truly under threat, only defending permits constant repeated attacks. Self-defense becomes a shield, whereas self-protection based on attack gives you a spear.

Many martial arts traditions recognize three psychological and physiological states related to physical encounters between you and an opponent: counterattacking, attacking while being attacked, and preemptive attack. These are listed in order of technical difficulty. Note that "attack" is used in all 3, it's the timing of your attack that differs.

Counterattacking is responding to an attack after receiving, intercepting, or blocking that of our opponent. The timing of actions in this scenario is often attack 1: block 1, and then counterattack 0.5. Attacking while being attacked occurs when we detect the unfolding threat and respond immediately during the opponent's attack. The timing of actions is attack 1: counterattack 1. Preemptive attack is taking action as soon as you perceive the opponent will attack but before they actually do. Subtle hints in body angle, visual gaze, breathing, and weight shift cue this. The timing of actions is preemptive counterattack -1: attack 0.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, the highest level is to perceive an imminent threat and take preventative action to avoid the scenario completely, but this is often impossible.

Not the first to strike, but the first to hit

When attacking for self-protection, you might successfully defeat an opponent, but it is 100% certain that it is harder for the opponent to attack you.

There are many scenarios where we don't want to hit, hurt, or harm someone. For example, a friend or family member whose capacity is altered by alcohol, drugs, or dementia. We want to avoid their violence but once we have a sufficient level of skill, we can hopefully do so without needing to strike.

You don't have to hit but you also aren't required to be hit. Attack-oriented, tactical body movement does not require you to strike, but it does keep you safe and put you in a good position to have many options.

Fist comes from the heart

So I revise the Cobra Kai mantra as "strike first, strike fast, show mercy" to align with the Wing Chun expression that "the fist comes from the heart". This saying means two things: 1) occupy the centre line and attack the opponent directly; and, 2) your attack is meant to stop the aggression and allow safety. We hurt with compassion and only harm if needed.

But our responses have to be done dispassionately; deliberately and without anger. As the original Miyagi (Miyagi Chojun, 1888-1953; founder of Goju-ryu karate) said "when anger rises the fists must lower, when you raise your fists you must lower your anger".

I can agree 100% with something else Mr. Miyagi said in Karate Kid II, though, that the best way to avoid a punch is to "not be there." But if we have no choice and have to be there, we must take the initiative. When the only way out is through, the best defense truly is a good offense.

(c) E. Paul Zehr (2026)

item.title: A Little Gratitude Can Go a Long Way at Work
item.description:
Gratitude

A Little Gratitude Can Go a Long Way at Work

What we notice at work shapes the culture we create.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude can help people feel seen, valued, and connected.
  • Gratitude matters in creating a workplace where people can do their best work.
  • Small, intentional acts of appreciation and gratitude practices can make a lasting difference.

We spend a significant portion of our waking hours at work. Beyond productivity and performance, our experience of those hours matters, too. Most of us know what it feels like to be appreciated and what it feels like when our efforts go unnoticed. When expressed genuinely, gratitude can help people feel seen, valued, and connected. It is a relational emotion that helps us recognize the contributions, kindness, and support we receive from others and gives us an opportunity to let them know that what they do matters. It’s also mutually beneficial! Expressing gratitude benefits both the giver and the receiver. Research suggests it can also:

  • Encourage helping: People who receive genuine thanks may be more likely to help others.
  • Support workplace well-being: Research reviews link gratitude with positive relationships, social support, and a healthier organizational climate.
  • Nurture individual well-being: Gratitude practices have been associated with improvements in well-being and positive emotions.

In our workplaces, moments of appreciation can strengthen our sense of value and belonging and contribute to a culture of respect where people may feel more comfortable asking questions and sharing ideas. Gratitude is not the only ingredient in psychological safety, but it can help create an environment where people feel supported. This makes a difference in our everyday work experience, and for organizations looking to retain talent and build teams that navigate challenges together.

Why Gratitude Matters, Especially When Things Are Changing

Many people find it easier to express and practice gratitude when things are going well. If your team is celebrating a big win, landing the client, closing the deal, or perhaps receiving an award, the appreciation may flow naturally. Yet the reality is that in the day-to-day, many organizations are also facing restructuring, navigating shifting priorities, operating with stretched resources, and people may just be trying to find their footing amid uncertainty.

People are not just moving through a change-management plan. They are experiencing change in a very real and personal way, on top of everything else they may already be carrying in their lives outside work. This is where gratitude encourages us to recognize people’s contributions while also acknowledging the realities they are navigating. The more intentionally we express gratitude, the more it flows through our teams and becomes part of our work culture, creating the conditions in which people can do the good work.

Ways to Bring More Gratitude Into the Workplace

1. Make your thank-you specific.

Take an extra moment to say “thank you” explicitly to those on your team. Hold eye contact and pause. Let the “thank you” land and sink in.

Or if you are connecting remotely, be specific in the email about what you are thankful for. For example, “Thank you for getting this report to me on time and in the format I asked for. This will help me with preparing for the next meeting.” Thank your manager for clarity and your colleagues for jumping in to support you in a moment you really needed it. Let them know what they did that made a difference.

2. Check in, and really listen.

Connect at least once a week, even with a simple message, email, or office pop-in. Ask how your teammates are doing, what is going well, and where they could use support. Listen to understand, not always to fix.

As leaders and teammates, we want our people to feel safe enough to learn, grow, take risks, and make mistakes. Yet, the reality is that no space is technically safe. It is the people in these spaces who can make us feel safe. A strategy that suggests that you are a safe individual people can talk to is to ask, “Do you need me to listen? Offer some advice? Intervene?”

3. Notice the progress and process, not just the outcome.

We are often more likely to celebrate the finished product than we are to recognize the collaboration, problem-solving, patience, creativity, and persistence that made it possible. Take time to acknowledge the person who asked the thoughtful question, helped a colleague get unstuck, or kept the team connected during a busy season. This helps people see that their everyday efforts make a difference.

4. Recognize people in the rooms they are not in.

Speak positively about colleagues’ contributions when they are not present. Give credit where it is due, share their ideas, and make their work visible. Being recognized for your good work boosts morale not just for the person being recognized, but others, too.

Gratitude can open doors and help build a culture where people advocate for and cheer one another on. Remember, the people at the top are collaborating. The people at the bottom are competing.

5. Ask what appreciation looks like to them.

Not everyone experiences appreciation in the same way. While some team members may value public shout-outs, others might prefer a private thank-you, a thoughtful email, or a handwritten note. For others, small gestures, like bringing them a coffee or a cookie unexpectedly, mean the most. Taking the time to ask what helps each person feel valued can ensure your appreciation truly resonates. What support would make their work more sustainable? What opportunities would help them grow? What would make the biggest difference to them right now? Sometimes, appreciation from a leader can mean opening the door to new opportunities for growth or giving someone the flexibility to attend their child’s school event or care for an aging parent.

Final Thoughts

If people on a team feel invisible, it’s harder for them to feel connected to a shared purpose, and when contributions consistently go unrecognized, people can be left feeling discouraged and disengaged. Gratitude is not a band-aid that can fix a broken system, replace fair compensation, ease unreasonable workloads, or provide real support. Yet when people feel seen and valued, it helps create the conditions for more positive and fulfilling workdays, and they are more likely to do their best work and bring their strengths forward.

Before moving on to your next task, I have one final gentle invitation: Who has made your work a little easier or your day a little better? Take a moment to tell them.

Our workdays are made up of many tasks, but we live them alongside others. Taking the time to notice, say thank you, and let people know they matter can have a lasting impact, not only on an individual level, but on the workplace culture created together.

item.title: Are Ideas Invented or Discovered?
item.description:
Creativity

Are Ideas Invented or Discovered?

Where ideas come from: a plausible answer to an age-old question

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • The invention view overlooks how unforseeable possibilities emerge during creation.
  • The discovered view overlooks how creators shape which possibilities become reality.
  • These views are reconciled using the notion of potentiality which incorporates probabilities of possibilities.
  • We hone an idea by seeing it from new perspectives, allowing it to potentially take unanticipated directions.

Where do ideas come from? The question has intrigued philosophers, scientists, and artists for centuries.

Mathematicians sometimes describe their findings as though they were exploring a landscape that existed long before they did. Composers speak of melodies that seem to come to them from somewhere beyond themselves. Writers sometimes find that their characters take on lives of their own, behaving in ways their creators hadn’t anticipated. Such experiences appear to support the discovered view, according to which a creative work exists in some abstract realm of possibilities, and its creator gradually uncovers it. This resembles Platonism: the idea that mathematical truths, and perhaps other abstract structures, exist independently of our awareness of them.

Yet it seems counterintuitive that if Shakespeare hadn’t written Hamlet, or Beethoven hadn’t composed his Fifth Symphony, these works would still have existed somewhere, waiting for someone else to find them. The discovered view is generally contrasted with the invented view, according to which it is the creator who brings the work into existence. In this view, when you write a story, you usher it into being with each decision you make about what happens next.

I think neither view precisely captures the creative process. To resolve this puzzle, we may need to reconsider something we usually take for granted: the nature of potentiality.

What Changes as a Work Takes Shape?

Imagine a sculptor contemplating an unhewn stone. Every sculpture that could be carved from it is “possible.” The stone could become a bear, a human, or abstract art. In this sense, each of the endless possibilities that are latent (i.e., that lie dormant) in the stone could be said to “exist.”

But these possibilities are not equally probable, and moreover, their relative probabilities shift as sculpting proceeds. The sculptor brings to the task particular interests and skills, as well as a predilection to pay attention to and be inspired by certain aspects of the stone. Perhaps a smooth bump suggests the curve of a delicate shoulder, and the sculptor starts envisioning it as an angel or ballerina. But as the carving proceeds, the sculptor notices that the middle of the region where the face should go is red, and becomes increasingly excited by the idea that the red region would make a great clown nose. Features such as an exaggerated smile and a flower-adorned cap, which were initially unlikely, become increasingly probable. Over time, the clown possibility becomes more likely, and conversely, as more stone is removed, other possibilities become physically impossible.

At each step of the journey, the sculptor’s next action is influenced by two factors: (1) the sculptor’s developing mental model (or conception) of the sculpture, and (2) the unfolding physical state of the unfinished sculpture itself. The interplay of these two factors results in the series of actions by which, out of endless initial possibilities, eventually just one remains.

In short, it’s in some sense true that the final sculpture in all its idiosyncratic detail existed as a possibility for that stone from the start. This appears to support the discovered view. However, it’s also true that the final clown sculpture did not exist in the sculptor’s mind as a well-defined option that got chosen from amongst other possible options. And this appears to support the invented view.

What gives?

Possibility Versus Potentiality

A potential resolution to this paradox can be found by turning from possibility to potentiality. The resolution proposed here is consistent with the theory that reality is potentiality as proposed in my last piece; however, it doesn’t depend on whether this theory is correct.

The stone had the potential to become the particular clown sculpture that eventually emerged, but initially this outcome was highly improbable. As sculpting proceeded, its probability increased, conditional on the evolving state of both the sculptor’s mind and the sculpture itself.

New possibilities need not come into existence for potentiality to change. Potentiality concerns not just what is possible, but the relative probabilities (or perhaps amplitudes) of different outcomes. These probabilities change as the creative process unfolds. Moreover, an initially vague idea need not consist of a set of well-defined possibilities; these may themselves become differentiated as the idea takes shape.

For example, when we write a story, devise a scientific explanation, or compose music, an idea may begin as a vague intuition, a sense that there’s something worth pursuing without knowing quite what it is. As we consider it from different perspectives, certain aspects come into focus, suggesting possibilities that hadn’t previously occurred to us. These possibilities may emerge from the depths of our unconscious, beyond reach until now, when we find ourselves in a situation where they’ve become relevant. They may have existed in principle all along, but their probability of being realized was formerly negligible.

Honing New Possibilities Into Existence

Honing theory, an account of creativity I’ve been developing for some time (discussed in detail in my book Dawn of the Creative Mind), proposes that creative ideas take shape through successive steps consisting of interactions between (1) the creator’s current internal conception of the idea, and (2) new perspectives or ways of looking at or thinking about it that come to mind (e.g., how would my teacher take it from here?). This interaction is often influenced by a tangible external expression of the idea, such as the sculpture (e.g., perhaps the red part could be a clown nose). Each such step alters the conception of the idea, making some potential outcomes more probable, and others less so.

These interactions are guided by the creator’s world-model: their integrated understanding of themselves and the world, including what they don’t understand or accept or are currently wrestling with. A world-model includes not just conscious elements that you can access voluntarily, but elements brewing below the threshold of awareness: a painful memory, forbidden desire, or simply a pattern or connection you’d perceived at some level but never before had any reason to bring to mind. For example, perhaps the sculptor had a fear of or admiration for clowns, and the experience of creating one from stone helps them come to terms with the fear or find their own “inner clown.” Thus, each new conception of the idea may, in turn, alter the creator’s world-model; creators speak of achieving a greater sense of wholeness or integration as they create.

Summing Up

This resolution to the “invented versus discovered” debate doesn’t definitively settle the question of whether every conceivable idea exists in some timeless abstract realm. It does, however, offer a way to reconcile the two traditional answers.

Creative works are invented to the extent that our decisions and actions shape what comes into existence, altering the relative probabilities of subsequent outcomes. And they’re discovered to the extent that possibilities emerge that we hadn’t anticipated, arising from interactions between our evolving conception of the work and new perspectives that come to mind, sometimes without conscious awareness. People who follow a preconceived path to the completion of their creative work (those whom creative writers refer to as “planners”) may resonate more with the invented view. Those who are more open to the new possibilities that spontaneously emerge as the creative process proceeds (those whom creative writers refer to as “pantsers,” as in “by the seat of their pants”) may resonate more with the discovered view.

The resolution proposed here also suggests that each traditional answer misses something essential about the creative process. The discovered view misses that whether something gets created depends not just on whether it is possible in theory, but on whether it becomes sufficiently probable within the creator’s mind to influence—consciously or unconsciously—the creative process. And the invented view misses that creators aren’t fully aware of the contents of their own minds, particularly possibilities that depend on conditions that haven’t arisen yet.

item.title: A Time for Courage
item.description:
Self-Help

A Time for Courage

Becoming risk-friendly through kindness

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Being courageous often means fearing the risks and acting anyway.
  • When acting courageously results in a negative outcome, it's important to be kind to ourselves.
  • Kindness can help us feel more comfortable being risk-friendly and free us from the perfectionism trap.
Harriet Tubman
Source: Smithsonian / Unsplash

Several older understandings of the word courage are associated with words related to “heart.” What can we make of this connection between courage and heart? We could say that it takes courage to follow our hearts. This can happen when we are determined to live in accord with a heartfelt value that isn’t popular. Our hearts can also get involved in other ways, helping us act courageously.

Courage, Fear and Risks

It may seem silly to suggest that a decision involving no fear and little or no risk somehow requires courage. An inherent relationship seems to exist between acting courageously, feeling fear, and taking a risk. A risk exists when a choice’s outcome could involve loss or danger. Courage involves feeling scared, facing that fear, and acting anyway.

Bringing Heartfelt Kindness to Acting Courageously

I have asked dozens and dozens of people what they feared when considering acting courageously. Inevitably, I heard the same response again and again. They feared an unfavorable outcome from the risk they took, that someone might be hurt or harmed.

I then asked another question: How do you feel about yourself when the outcome of your choice is unfavorable? People responded similarly, saying they felt inadequate, stupid, unforgivable, incompetent, and unlovable. I quickly noticed that my own experience mirrored theirs. We responded to an inauspicious result not simply with remorse or sorrow, but by launching disparaging remarks about our characters.

What Do We Really Fear?

Obviously, we’re not eager for an adverse outcome of the courageous action we undertake. However, even when asked, with the same information, would you take the same action again? Most people were ready to do it again. I then asked, with the same unfavorable outcome, would you beat yourself up again? The response was, “I likely would.”

We are certainly concerned about the outcomes of our choices. However, unless something tragic happens, we seem to fear how harshly we will treat ourselves when something less than positive occurs. It makes taking a risk and calling for courage much less appealing.

The practice is to offer yourself kindness when the consequences of your choices aren’t highly advantageous. Maybe suffering through the results is plenty. We can feel regret and sadness. We don’t need to turn against ourselves, too. Such mistreatment doesn’t make us better at making choices. When we believe we will do our best to remain kind to ourselves, we become more risk-friendly and more ready to face our fears courageously.

An Extra Benefit of Kindness

Kindness can also relieve the endless striving of perfectionism. When an adverse consequence can define our worth, we either cut back on taking risks or embrace future risks with the possibility of redemption. The latter option is what drives perfectionism. If we refuse to attack ourselves after a less-than-auspicious outcome, we can appreciate acting courageously without any guarantee of a particular outcome. Being kind to ourselves frees us from an endless quest to get life right, reminding us that, through kindness, we’re getting ourselves right and, if we’re lucky, letting life help with the process.

We live at a time of unparalleled divisiveness. It results in surviving rather than thriving. As trust erodes, we focus more on protecting ourselves from accusations coming from across the aisle. We also devote time and energy to launching our own aggressive attacks. Tribalism walls us off from beliefs and values different from ours, and we lose the deep sense of belonging that unity consciousness provides. The fences that separate us from others can also separate us from ourselves.

Kindness. Yes, kindness is the medicine that helps us be more risk-friendly, more courageous, and more willing to make peace with our imperfect humanity. Maybe unity consciousness can begin as an inside job.

item.title: 2 Factors That Actually Make a “Fluid Relationship” Work
item.description:
Relationships

2 Factors That Actually Make a “Fluid Relationship” Work

A fluid relationship isn't fantasy fiction, but it does take effort.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Fluid relationships prioritize partners’ evolving needs, not rules about exclusivity.
  • Accepting a partner does not mean excusing harmful behavior or abandoning boundaries.
  • Flexibility in relationships only works with clear communication, mutual respect, and shared values.
Source: Judd Mauricio / Pexels

Not long ago, relationships largely followed a traditional narrative. They followed fairly predictable stages and expectations—dating, marriage, and a shared household—all bounded by set, often unspoken, rules.

However, a new wave of acceptance and open-mindedness has ushered in an era where love isn’t bound by convention. The recognition and acceptance of same-sex couples, once a taboo in many cultures, is now largely celebrated. Similarly, open relationships, once whispered about in hushed tones, are finding vocal proponents. Furthermore, living-apart-together marriages challenge the age-old belief that marital success is rooted in cohabitation.

A combination of factors, including cultural shifts, increasing global connectivity, and a strong desire for personal authenticity, seems to be driving this change. As people are exposed to diverse cultures and ideas, there’s a growing realization that “one size does not fit all” when it comes to relationships. Moreover, with mental health and individual well-being taking center stage, there’s a heightened focus on relationships that truly cater to emotional needs rather than fitting a societal mold. The beauty of this evolution is that it paves the way for more authentic self-expression—which is where the concept of a “fluid relationship” comes in.

Compared to other types of relationships, both traditional and non-traditional, a fluid relationship has two key characteristics that make it an attractive option for people who want to settle down without having to settle down.

1. It Prioritizes the Independent Emotional and Physical Needs of the Partners

Unlike open relationships, where there’s often an explicit understanding about external partners, fluid relationships aren’t primarily defined by the presence or absence of other sexual or romantic partners. The bond between the primary partners may transcend these factors, emphasizing emotional connection, mutual growth, or other unique dynamics tailored to their needs.

For example, if the relationship is going through a dead-bedroom episode, consensual non-monogamy is an option the partners are willing to discuss in a fluid relationship. In a traditional relationship, perhaps the focus would be on working through the lack of intimacy with each other via therapy. While this is effective, it’s a process that can be slow and time-intensive. The other option, which unfortunately happens in such cases, is infidelity.

Opening up a relationship, while it may sound like a recipe for disaster, carries less risk than you might think as long as you and your partner are on the same page about why you are doing it. A 2020 study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science found that opening up a relationship did not necessarily lead to decreased life satisfaction or relationship quality in couples who did so primarily because they were sexually incompatible with their partners.

2. There’s a Deep Emphasis on Being Flexible and Adaptable

The very essence of a “fluid” relationship is its capacity for change. It acknowledges the ebb and flow of life, ensuring the relationship remains relevant and supportive. Whether it’s navigating through temporary long-distance phases, changes in life priorities, or personal growth trajectories, a fluid relationship is resilient, molding itself to the evolving needs of the partners involved.

A 2020 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Contextual Behavioral Science found that people who were inflexible often had poor relationship outcomes. They were more likely to have weaker bonds with their partners, have poorer sex lives, and resort to unhealthy relationship behaviors like shouting, screaming, and domestic violence.

With a fluid relationship, both partners know that the relationship is built on adapting to situations. If either partner encounters behaviors in the other they aren’t happy with, there is a common understanding between them that they are not bound by the relationship to fix the issue. This opens up new avenues to remedy conflict.

While some differences between partners can be worked through, accepting your partner for who they are is a given in fluid relationships. Of course, this doesn’t mean partners are given a pass for any and all behavior—and open communication is a necessity in any relationship, fluid or otherwise.

Take the example of the incident with Grimes and Shivon Zilis, who are both linked to Elon Musk romantically. Although Grimes has called her relationship with Musk “fluid,” she was upset when she found out about his twins with Zilis in 2021, along with the rest of the world. The two women have since cleared the air and appear to be on good terms with each other, judging by their interactions on social media. Grimes’ main gripe seemed to be with how the information was communicated to her, not the information itself.

The episode underscores the premise that fluid relationships, while offering flexibility, also demand genuine work and mutual respect. Relationships, regardless of how they’re labeled, require effort, understanding, and, often, a lot of patience.

In the evolving landscape of relationships, the allure of fluidity offers the promise of authenticity and adaptability. However, as with all forms of partnerships, its success lies in the bedrock of clear communication, mutual respect, and shared values. At its heart, a fluid relationship isn’t just about being adaptable; it’s about creating a space where both partners feel valued, understood, and free to evolve together. Whether or not one opts for this approach, the overarching goal remains the same: cultivating a bond that nurtures and enriches both individuals involved.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: 7 Signs You're in Denial
item.description:
Denial

7 Signs You're in Denial

How to get out of your own bubble.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • We deny what makes us uncomfortable, ashamed, or unhappy.
  • Yet denial often lasts too long to be useful or healthy.
  • Knowing the 7 signs and 7 solutions can help us face reality sooner.
Source: AI-generated

“It’s not happening,” you tell yourself. But you know it is. It’s just easier to look the other way, assign blame, ignore advice, and bury your head.

Whether facing redundancy, infidelity, or death, we don’t realize we’re in denial, refusing to accept threatening or disruptive reality.

But the mythical ostrich must eventually raise its head. What it sees depends on how long it has stayed down and what happened in the meantime. The result of this ultimate defense mode is not only missed moments but lost credibility, and frequently, regret.

So how does it start?

Egotism can play a contributing role. Proud people don’t want to accept that their views or interpretation of the world are flawed. We want to believe our children never lie, parents will live forever, and colleagues want us to succeed.

In her book, Margaret Heffernan calls it willful blindness. It’s a blind spot and deaf spot combined. We see and hear only what we want. Yet there’s a difference between hope and denial. Hope says, “This might work out,” while denial says, “This isn’t happening.”

The self-deception is fueled by wishful thinking and low coping skills. Deniers may feel they can’t manage the upheaval, shame, or pain. Often, that’s true. Golman, Hagmann and Loewenstein refer to information avoidance. It may seem more attractive. Yet procrastination simply defers inevitable adjustment.

The underlying process of denial often appears similar, whether it’s a failing marriage, impending redundancy or a dying relative. But the emotion, social consequences and responses differ.

How to Recognise and Respond to Denial

Seven signals suggest you’re living in a protected bubble. Before considering the solutions offered by behavioral science, ask yourself if you repeat any of these narratives. Is there a pattern? If several sound familiar, take note.

The first four signals relate to dismissing disconfirming evidence.

  1. “You must be wrong.”

We tune out contrarian voices, despite experience, history, or factual evidence. It’s status-agnostic. People hate bad news. For instance, research finds investors don’t review their accounts as frequently in a bear market. A person who dismisses repeated financial warnings as “bad luck” assumes others are wrong.

What to do? Ask what would make you change your mind. If no new data point or advice persuades you to shift, you’re in denial mode and likely downgrading others’ opinions.

  1. “That’s nonsense.”

We live in denial when we dismiss contrary arguments, advice, or opinion, and only prioritize data consistent with beliefs. A bad manager thinks resigning employees are ‘bitter leavers.’ Some CEOs, politicians and even Presidents are convinced about their fitness for office despite popular opinion.

Look for patterns, not just exceptions. Count and date events as a record. One happy client doesn’t cancel the need to review ten unhappy clients. The trend reveals the truth, as occasionally peers do.

  1. “What do peers think?”
Source: AI-generated

People in denial tend to shrink their circle to those who agree with them. This echo chamber shows up in the workplace, church hall, and sports club.

We seek selective exposure to like-minded thinkers. Similarly, conspiracy theorists and climate deniers all believe they’re right.

Escaping the bubble means inviting perspectives from dissenters. They have less to lose by telling you the truth. And usually, are delighted to do so.

  1. “They haven’t a clue.”

People in denial shoot the messenger. Deniers can belittle naysayers, ridicule or even attack dissenters as clueless, misinformed, jealous, or intellectually inferior. Sometimes, all of the above. They refuse to discuss the controversial topic, protecting their comforting view. The more emotionally distressing the reality, the greater the denial, like hearing the diagnosis of a terminally ill child or parental decline.

Science suggests a solution. One evidence-based strategy is to consider the opposite view. Professional debaters do this convincingly. Research shows this can reduce misjudgment and singular perspectives.

The next two signs involve avoidance and delay.

  1. “It’s just a one-off.”

People living in a bubble minimize contrary arguments or trivialize warnings until it’s too late. When we’re in denial mode, we consider any unethical transgression, suspicious absence, ‘working late’ excuse, or bank account anomaly a one-off. The same goes for medical complaints. “It’s only a crusty freckle, not a potential melanoma.” We justify the position and make excuses.

Set a tripwire. You can decide in advance what will trigger action. For instance, “If the freckle changes, I book the appointment.” Or “If the transgression is material, I’ll report it.”

  1. “I’ll deal with it later.”
Source: AI-generated

We defer action, from refusing to fix a leaky tap to admitting gambling or alcoholism. It becomes about timing.

You won’t address it ‘yet’. But ‘not yet’ never ends.

Explore what’s stopping the acceptance of reality. By naming the fear aloud, you give it focus. Fear tends to shrink when it has both an identifiable label and a deadline.

  1. “That’s not me.”

The final sign concerns identity. We see the denial tendency in others far quicker than ourselves. If you’re now thinking of someone else, look within. It’s a blind spot.

A simple solution exists. Ask someone you trust, “What am I not seeing?” Don’t argue. Just listen and consider if it might be true. Denying redundancy or bereavement makes us miserable for longer.

As I write in TUNE IN: How to Make Smarter Decisions in a Noisy World, behavioral solutions seem obvious to the misjudgment problem. The problem is we tune in too late.

Some argue denial has value. It protects in a crisis. Taylor and Brown argue that positive illusions can support wellbeing. Buying time can be a temporary band-aid. The cost of avoidance depends on the depth and duration of denial. A missed cancer diagnosis or failed marriage could have been prevented; a loved one might have had a more meaningful goodbye.

All seven signs of denial reveal something we’re actively resisting and rationalizing. The ostrich doesn’t bury its head. We do. Turning a blind eye or a deaf ear hurts more in the long run.

It’s time to burst the bubble.

item.title: Why "I Understand" Can Make Someone Feel Misunderstood
item.description:
Cognition

Why "I Understand" Can Make Someone Feel Misunderstood

You can understand what someone means without knowing how it felt.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Claiming to know how someone feels can unintentionally make them feel more misunderstood.
  • Research suggests that accurately knowing someone doesn't necessarily make them feel understood.
  • By adopting the not-knowing stance, you allow someone to remain the authority on their own experience.
  • Empathy requires humility about what cannot be known and confidence in what can be understood.

Have you ever told someone, "I understand", only for them to respond:

No, you don't! How could you possibly understand? You haven't been through what I've been through.

Yet, you've listened carefully, tried to appreciate their perspective, and offered what you thought was a reassuring expression of empathy.

But still, somehow, your attempt to make them feel understood has achieved the opposite.

Why Can “I Understand” Provoke Such a Response?

Because of the difference between two kinds of understanding:

  • Understanding what someone is communicating: grasping what they're trying to tell you — their thoughts, feelings, perspective, and the meaning they attach to an experience.
  • Understanding what someone has experienced: knowing what it actually felt like to live through that experience — a subjective perspective you can never fully inhabit.

You Can Understand What Someone Means Without Understanding Their Lived Experience

Imagine someone telling you about a particularly difficult period in their life.

As they speak, you appreciate what they're trying to communicate. You hear about the difficulties they faced and why they found the experience so upsetting.

Then, hoping to show some empathy, you say:

I understand how you feel.

Although you may understand what they're telling you, can you truly know what their experience felt like?

Not entirely.

Even if you've been through something remarkably similar, your experience will never be identical. Your history, personality, and circumstances all influence how events are experienced and interpreted.

So they may interpret your words as a claim to know something that cannot be fully known.

Now compare that with saying:

I understand what you mean.

Rather than claiming to know what their experience felt like, you're acknowledging that you've understood what they're trying to communicate.

Why Understanding Someone Doesn't Always Make Them Feel Understood

In their review of feeling understood in relationships, psychologist Harry Reis and colleagues distinguished between two different types of understanding:1

  • Actual understanding: How accurately another person understands someone's thoughts, feelings and experiences.
  • Perceived understanding: How much that person feels understood by someone else.

The two aren’t as related as you might think. In a study involving 199 newlywed couples, psychologists Monique Pollmann and Catrin Finkenauer found that how accurately partners knew one another was largely unrelated to how understood they felt.2

In fact, perceived understanding predicted relationship wellbeing, whereas actual understanding did not.

The Importance of Knowing What Cannot Be Known

The developers of Mentalization-based Treatment, Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy, emphasise the importance of adopting a not-knowing stance, recognising that another person's mental world can never be entirely accessible to us.3

People can make educated guesses about what someone might be thinking or feeling, but these interpretations are always open to correction.

For example, telling someone who wasn’t invited to a party, "You must have felt rejected", imposes an interpretation of their experience.

Asking "How did that make you feel?" allows them to describe their experience in their own words.

Even when offering your own interpretation, phrasing it tentatively as a question — such as "Did that leave you feeling rejected?" — gives them room to confirm or correct it.

By adopting the not-knowing stance, you allow someone to remain the authority on their own experience.

You Don't Need to Have Experienced What Someone Has Experienced to Understand What They're Telling You

For example:

  • You don't need to have experienced bereavement to understand someone describing how much they miss a loved one.
  • You don't need to have experienced discrimination to understand someone explaining why they found an interaction humiliating.
  • You don't need to have experienced a mental illness to understand someone describing how it affects their everyday life.

You can:

  • listen to someone's account,
  • recognise the emotions they're expressing,
  • appreciate the meaning they attribute to their experience, and
  • acknowledge why it matters to them.

How to Make Someone Feel Understood

The next time someone shares a meaningful experience, rather than immediately reassuring them that their feelings are understood, demonstrate that what they're communicating has been understood.

For example, imagine someone says:

I'm so tired of people telling me what I should do. Nobody seems interested in actually listening to me.

Instead of responding with, "I understand how you feel", try:

I understand what you mean. It sounds like people keep offering you solutions when what you really want is for someone to hear your perspective.

Instead of claiming their experience, you’re recognising it.

Other useful expressions include:

  • "I see what you're saying."
  • "I think I understand what you mean."
  • "From what you're telling me, it sounds like..."
  • "That helps explain why this has been so important to you."
  • "Have I understood that correctly?"

The Paradox of Making People Feel Understood

You might think that the more confidently you communicate your understanding, the more understood another person will feel. But often, the opposite is true.

The more certain you become that you understand another person’s experience, the less curious you may become about what that experience actually means to them.

The key is to balance humility about what you cannot know with confidence in what you can understand.

So the next time someone shares something meaningful, remember that you don’t need to have lived their experience to understand what they’re trying to tell you.

Making someone feel understood requires less certainty about what they feel and more curiosity about what they’re trying to communicate.
